planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into wet to moist, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy soil in full sun to light shade; fringed meadow beauty is the smallest Rhexia and is easily crowded, so give it open, low-competition bog margins rather than dense plantings.

directions: Fringed meadow beauty is the smallest and most delicate of the southeastern Rhexia species, forming low, wiry clumps under a foot tall with distinctly petioled, ciliate-margined leaves that give the species its common name. It grows in wet pine flatwoods and savannas, pocosin borders, cypress pond edges, and coastal swales from Texas to Maryland, always in acidic, moist to wet, nutrient-poor sandy soil in full to partial sun. From late spring through summer it produces small but showy pink, four-petaled flowers with the urn-shaped hypanthium typical of the genus, opening for a single morning and pollinated by buzzing bees that vibrate loose the pollen from the curved yellow anthers. Because it is so compact and easily shaded out, site it at the open, sunny edge of a bog garden rather than among taller wetland companions, and never fertilize it — like its relatives it is adapted to poor, acidic soils and declines in enriched ground.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Rhexia petiolata

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy soil in full sun; yellow meadow beauty is the only yellow-flowered Rhexia and needs the same constantly saturated seepage-slope conditions as its pink-flowered relatives.

directions: Yellow meadow beauty is the sole member of its genus with true yellow flowers, an immediate identification feature that sets it apart from the pink- and rose-flowered Rhexia species that share its habitat. It is a low, bushy, colonial perennial of wet pine flatwoods and savannas, seepage slopes, and bogs along the Coastal Plain from eastern North Carolina south to Florida and west into the Gulf states, spreading by rhizomes into loose patches where conditions stay reliably wet. The stiff-hairy, four-angled stems bear narrow, three-veined leaves and small axillary flowers with four broad yellow petals rising from the hairy, urn-shaped hypanthium characteristic of all meadow beauties, blooming through summer and drawing the same buzz-pollinating bees that work its pink relatives. It will not tolerate a habitat that dries out, so reserve it for a permanently saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor bog planting alongside pitcher plants and other Rhexia species, where its color break adds real variety to a native meadowbeauty collection.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Rhexia lutea
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant corms from nursery-propagated sources in spring in wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, nutrient-poor soil in full sun; pale grass-pink is smaller-flowered than its more common relative Calopogon tuberosus and often flowers heavily the season after a bog is burned or mowed.

directions: Pale grass-pink is a smaller, more delicate cousin of the common grass-pink orchid, distinguished by its narrower, paler pink to nearly white flowers with reflexed sepals and a tuft of yellow bristles on the upward-facing lip. It grows from a single grasslike basal leaf and slender flower stalk in wet flatwoods, bogs, pinelands, and roadside savannas across the southeastern Coastal Plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Louisiana, often flowering most abundantly in the seasons following a fire that opens up the bog canopy. Like the other Calopogon, it practices deceptive pollination — naive bees land on the hairy lip expecting a nectar reward, tip it downward under their weight, and fall onto the true pollen masses below — so plants depend on inexperienced pollinators and do not offer a nectar reward. Site nursery-propagated corms in permanently wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy or peaty soil in full sun alongside pitcher plants and sundews, and avoid any fertilizer or soil amendment.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in mucky or shallowly flooded, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; fringed yellow-eyed grass is by far the largest and showiest eastern Xyris, reaching up to five feet in bloom, and needs sustained wetness at the pond or ditch margin.

directions: Fringed yellow-eyed grass is the giant of its genus, sending up olive-green, grass-like leaves to nearly two feet and wiry flowering stalks that can reach four to five feet, tipped by an oval spike whose bracts have conspicuously fringed, fuzzy-looking keels. In early fall it opens bright three-petaled yellow flowers a few at a time each morning, held well above the surrounding vegetation, an unusually tall and architectural presence for a bog garden. It occurs in the mucky or sandy margins of upland depression ponds, sandhill seepage streams, impoundments, and wet ditches on the Coastal Plain from Texas to New Jersey, always in standing or saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor water. Give it a permanently wet to shallowly flooded planting pocket in full sun at the edge of a bog pool alongside pipewort and pitcher plants, and avoid fertilizing, since it is adapted to naturally infertile wetland soils.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — Fringed Yelloweyed Grass

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in wet to seasonally moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; coastal plain yellow-eyed grass is one of the most common and adaptable Xyris of pine savannas and tolerates slightly drier bog margins than most of its relatives.

directions: Coastal plain yellow-eyed grass forms a fan of broadly linear, slightly twisted, blunt-tipped leaves with slick, mucilaginous bases, from which wiry stalks up to three feet rise bearing dense oval spikes that open a few bright yellow, three-petaled flowers each morning through summer. It is among the most widespread and abundant Xyris of the wet pine savannas and flatwoods, depression pond edges, bog margins, and lakeshores across the southeastern and south-central United States from Texas to Virginia and inland to Tennessee and Arkansas, growing in moist sandy peat that ranges from shallowly flooded to seasonally just-damp. That tolerance for periods of lesser saturation makes it a forgiving Xyris for the drier fringes of a home bog garden, though it still performs best in full sun on constantly acidic, nutrient-poor sand. Pair it with pitcher plants, sundews, and meadow beauties for an authentic wet-savanna planting, and skip fertilizer entirely, since enriched soil favors weeds over this lean-soil specialist.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow standing water or saturated, acidic, sandy peat in full sun; flattened pipewort's flower heads are noticeably soft and compressible compared to the stiffer heads of ten-angle pipewort, its more commonly grown relative.

directions: Flattened pipewort produces a low rosette of oblong to elliptic leaves and slender, ribbed flower stalks topped by small, button-like white flower heads from late spring through fall; the heads are distinctly soft and squeeze flat between finger and thumb when fresh, the trait behind both its common and scientific names, unlike the firmer heads of the larger ten-angle pipewort it often grows alongside. It occurs in ponds, lakes, and other shallow depressions, the wetter pockets of pine flatwoods and savannas, acidic seeps, and Atlantic white cedar swamps along the Coastal Plain from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Texas, typically standing in an inch or two of acidic, nutrient-poor water. Give it a permanently flooded or saturated planting pocket at the shallow margin of a bog pool in full sun, matching the same low-fertility, acidic conditions required by pitcher plants and sundews, and never fertilize — added nutrients quickly let algae and weeds overtake this specialized wetland native.
sources: Native Plant Trust Go Botany — Eriocaulon compressum
